extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, and agency officials
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating reforms to administrative agencies that institutionalize contestation, broaden participation, and prevent the closure of political conflict (e.g., opening agendas, hardwiring conflict, identity-conscious processes, and reconsidering nationwide injunctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening the regulatory agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Make agenda control more “open access” so agencies must engage questions they might otherwise ignore; reduce agencies’ near monopoly over the regulatory agenda and force engagement even where agencies would prefer to ignore issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include enabling and responding to rulemaking petitions, advisory committees, focus groups, listening sessions, and internet forums. Institutionalize and enforce the use of these tools broadly rather than deploying them fleetingly. Be mindful that opening agendas risks strategic flooding of issues and resource-allocation interference; reforms should balance openness with operational capacity. Empirical studies show agencies ignore many petitions and respond to statutory calls for rulemaking less than half the time; reforms should address that responsiveness gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and institutionalization of participatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and institutionalize existing participatory devices (rulemaking petitions, advisory committees, focus groups, listening sessions, internet forums) to cede some control of the agenda to stakeholder groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices can be effective if implemented with care and attention to participatory imbalances. Examples: IRS Priority Guidance Plan (annual solicitation of public priorities), FERC Office of Public Participation. ACUS recommends agencies engage affected and underrepresented groups on alternatives at the earliest stage. Avoid one-off or purely symbolic uses; instead build systematic application across agency business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and empower Offices of Public Participation / intervenor funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish dedicated institutional units (e.g., FERC’s Office of Public Participation) and consider programs like intervenor funding to make it easier for underrepresented members of the public to insert perspectives into agency proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices should aim to make processes inclusive, fair, and easy to navigate and consider funding to reduce resource barriers to participation. Explore interventions like FERC OPP’s study of intervenor funding and emulate models that actively recruit and support marginalized participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardwiring conflict into agency processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent closure of politics by deliberately embedding contestation into routine agency work—seek out excluded arguments and perspectives even when no one voices dissent, and invert tendencies to seek consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two central features: (1) ensure no decision is presumptively permanent (regular/continuing reevaluation); (2) ensure reevaluation episodes represent the full range of potential perspectives. Counteract self-censorship and preference falsification by proactively searching for latent dissent. Examples of institutional techniques include retrospective review, sunsets, regulatory contrarians, ombudsmen, and inspectors general. Avoid making every decision merely advisory by calibrating frequency and scope of reevaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective review and regulatory sunsetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutionalize retrospective review of existing policies at specified points and use sunset provisions to trigger periodic reauthorization and political contestation over rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective review’s purpose is to 'find things to complain about and fix them'—it fits agonistic aims. Sunsets can force reexamination but can bias toward deregulatory outcomes if agencies face roadblocks to promulgating replacement policies; pair sunsets with reforms that clear such roadblocks. Consider 'regulatory hammers' (automatic reversion to a stringent rule if agencies fail to produce a nuanced replacement) as complementary tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory contrarians and institutional watchdogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ or strengthen roles like ombudsmen, independent inspectors general, and other 'regulatory contrarians' whose function is to highlight blind spots and dissenting perspectives within agency decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These offices can be internal mechanisms to ensure contestation and to surface issues otherwise missed. They are common in state-level utility regulation (offices representing consumers). Scholarship provides typologies and examples; implementers should define contrarians’ mandates and protect their independence to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agonistic stance toward nationwide injunctions (percolation vs. contestation)
rubrics_metrics.description: From an agonistic perspective, nationwide injunctions are objectionable because they short-circuit opportunities for broader democratic contestation by preventing multiple plaintiffs in different forums from litigating and generating political contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits (clarity, effective relief for resource-poor plaintiffs via virtual representation) against costs (diminished opportunities for contestation/percolation). Agonistic theory favors limiting nationwide injunctions to preserve multiple fora for contestation and suggests subsidizing other forms of participation (e.g., legal aid) to address distributional concerns rather than relying on one plaintiff to extinguish national debate. Recognize counterarguments: percolation can produce high-quality legal development; distributional fairness may counsel continued use of nationwide relief in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational balancing and identity-conscious participatory processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Broaden access to equity and justice by designing participatory processes that deliberately identify, recruit, and amplify marginalized and excluded voices so that their resistance and claims for justice are treated as democratic politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast notice-and-comment and other participation mechanisms to seek out and amplify dissenting perspectives rather than passively sampling the public. Institutionalize identity-conscious mechanisms (e.g., reserved seats, specially constituted advisory councils) to counteract skewed participation. This approach accepts that remedial, identity-conscious processes may sometimes constrain majority will in service of democratic inclusion and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurpose notice-and-comment to amplify dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform notice-and-comment rulemaking from a passive information-sampling exercise into an active mechanism designed to find and amplify dissenting and marginalized perspectives, preventing false consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively identify interests, communities, and perspectives likely absent or underrepresented and ensure formal mechanisms to hear them. Reject designs that aim primarily to forge consensus; instead, embrace contestation as a core aim. Examples of experimental improvements include Regulation Room and proposals for interactive comment features (e.g., upvoting) to enhance deliberation, but the central aim should be systematic outreach to marginalized voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage federal advisory committees and FACA's 'fairly balanced' rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Use federal advisory committees (subject to FACA) to ensure decision-making bodies are 'fairly balanced in terms of the view represented' and reserve seats for specific affected groups to secure underrepresented perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FDA patient representatives on advisory committees; Bureau of Land Management resource advisory councils with tribal representatives; National Environmental Justice Advisory Council constituted to advance a particular perspective. Extend these design principles to other participatory processes (including notice-and-comment) to institutionalize representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted outreach and use of focus groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct targeted outreach to important stakeholder communities and use focus groups to purposively identify and recruit members of particular groups and to gauge reactions, alternatives, and concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement formal comment processes with targeted outreach and purposive sampling to ensure perspectives likely to be missing are included. Focus groups can surface preferred alternatives and early concerns; agencies should systematize such outreach rather than treating it as ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize attention to participatory imbalances
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement reforms with explicit attention to participatory imbalances—recognize and correct for the fact that some constituencies are better organized, resourced, or less subject to self-censorship than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS and scholars highlight the need to target affected groups that are often underrepresented and may suffer disproportionate harms. Practical steps: mandatory outreach requirements, reserved representation, subsidized participation (legal aid or intervenor funding), and continuous monitoring of who participates and whose views are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address distributional barriers to contestation (legal aid and subsidized participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and remediate the resource inequalities that limit some individuals' ability to litigate or participate; consider subsidizing participation (legal aid, intervenor funding) rather than relying solely on procedural or doctrinal fixes like nationwide injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nationwide injunctions can provide virtual representation for those lacking resources but may undercut broader opportunities for contestation; alternatives include increased legal aid, intervenor funding programs, and other subsidies to expand real participation. Design reforms to balance access-to-court concerns with the agonistic value of multiple forums for contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject consensus-forcing deliberative mechanisms when they suppress contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid participatory designs whose explicit aim is to forge consensus (e.g., some deliberative models, negotiated rulemaking) when the normative goal is to surface conflict and protect excluded perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While deliberative reforms seek to make public consultation more meaningful, agonistic prescriptions prioritize amplifying conflict. Historical evidence shows negotiated rulemaking often fails and may be anathema to targeted outreach aimed at generating contestation; design processes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance administrative capacity with openness to avoid strategic flooding
rubrics_metrics.description: When opening agenda-setting and amplifying participation, guard against the risk that strategic actors could overwhelm agencies by flooding them with issues the agency lacks resources to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain some agenda control to preserve functionality; calibrate openness (e.g., triage mechanisms, prioritization protocols like IRS Priority Guidance Plan) so agencies engage legitimate concerns without being debilitated. Administrative law traditionally hesitates to interfere with agenda setting because of resource allocation concerns—reforms should address those concerns explicitly.
